title: Sketches by Boz, Illustrative of Every-Day Life and Every-Day People
description: Dickens's first book: fifty-six sketches, mostly reprinted from the Monthly Magazine, the Morning Chronicle and the Evening Chronicle, issued in two series (first series February 1836, second December 1836) with illustrations by George Cruikshank. The pieces fall into four groups: sketches of London streets, of 'characters', of 'scenes' and of private life, and they invent the method of the later novels — the observing reporter's eye, the comic inventory of metropolitan types, and the sentimental vignette of the poor.
plot_or_argument: There is no continuous narrative. The 'Scenes' section follows a London day from morning to night, the 'Characters' section presents a gallery of types (the beadle, the parish clerk, the hospital patient, the 'gentleman' in reduced circumstances), and the 'Tales' section includes the first version of the story later worked into The Pickwick Papers, 'A Dinner at Poplar Walk'.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
literary_form: Collected periodical sketches in two series
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The 1830s London of the new police and the new penny press, of coaching inns giving way to the railways, and of a reading public created by the cheap miscellany. Dickens was a parliamentary reporter for the Mirror of Parliament and the True Sun while writing them.
literary_significance: Sketches by Boz established the pseudonym, the market and the subject of Dickens's whole career, and it is the first sustained attempt in English to write the modern city as a series of close-up notations rather than as a panorama.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1836, as collected periodical sketches in two series, by Charles Dickens. The title is also recorded as Sketches by Boz. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Pickwick Papers
alternative_titles: The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club
description: The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club, published in twenty monthly parts from March 1836 to October 1837, began as a commission to supply letterpress for Robert Seymour's sporting plates and became, after Seymour's suicide in April 1836 and the arrival of 'Phiz' (Hablot K. Browne), the first great popular success of the Victorian serial novel.
plot_or_argument: Mr Samuel Pickwick, founder of the Pickwick Club, sets out with his three fellows — Tracy Tupman, Nathaniel Winkle and Augustus Snodgrass — to travel England and report on their observations. The early chapters are a sequence of comic disasters at the club's expense; the entrance of Sam Weller as Pickwick's servant gives the book its double act, and the plot thickens into the breach-of-promise action brought by Mrs Bardell, Pickwick's landlady, which sends him to the Fleet Prison rather than pay the damages. The interpolated tales (the 'Bagman's Story', 'A Madman's Manuscript') darken the comic surface, and the ending restores Pickwick to Dingley Dell and to a bachelor old age surrounded by his friends.
narrative_structure: Twenty monthly numbers of loose episodic narrative, unified by the Pickwick Club frame and by the Bardell lawsuit, with interpolated tales inset at intervals.
principal_characters: Samuel Pickwick; Sam Weller; Tony Weller; Nathaniel Winkle; Tracy Tupman; Augustus Snodgrass; Mrs Bardell; Alfred Jingle; Mr Perker; Serjeant Buzfuz
literary_form: Comic novel in monthly parts (20 numbers, 1836-37)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The reforming 1830s: the new poor law of 1834, the reformed Parliament, the coaching inn and the stagecoach at the moment of the railway, and the legal system of the Fleet and the King's Bench prisons. The book's comedy of clubs, elections and litigiousness is also a satire on the unreformed institutions the Reform Act had not touched.
literary_significance: The Pickwick Papers created the Victorian bestseller and the monthly-part system, and with it the idea of a national comic fiction readable aloud in the family. Its sales (40,000 a number at the height of the run) made publishers understand the economics of serialisation for the rest of the century, and Sam Weller's speech became a permanent English idiom.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly shilling numbers from March 1836 to November 1837, with plates first by Robert Seymour and, after his death, by Hablot K. Browne ('Phiz'); the full title on the wrapper is The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Oliver Twist; or, The Parish Boy's Progress
description: Dickens's second novel and the first English novel to make the workhouse child its hero, serialised in Bentley's Miscellany from February 1837 (while Pickwick was still running) and published in three volumes in November 1838, with illustrations by George Cruikshank.
plot_or_argument: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse, spends his infancy in a branch workhouse under Mrs Mann, and at nine is returned to the main house, where he asks for more gruel and is apprenticed to an undertaker. He runs away to London, is taken up by the Artful Dodger and Fagin, is briefly in the hands of the burglar Bill Sikes and his dog, is shot and sheltered by the Maylies, and is then kidnapped back by Fagin and Nancy; Nancy's warning to Mr Brownlow and her murder by Sikes lead to the exposure of the plot of Monks, Oliver's half-brother, and to Oliver's restoration to his inheritance.
narrative_structure: Third-person narrative with a double plot — the parish boy's progress and the exposure of Monks's conspiracy — organised as a series of institutions (workhouse, undertaker's, thieves' kitchen, Maylie household) through which the hero passes.
principal_characters: Oliver Twist; Fagin; Nancy; Bill Sikes; the Artful Dodger; Mr Bumble; Mr Brownlow; Rose Maylie; Monks; Mr Grimwig
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, the workhouse system and the reportage of the Poor Law Commissioners, the criminal underworld of Field Lane and Saffron Hill, and the antisemitic conventions of the stage Jew which the character of Fagin reproduces and to which Dickens later responded in Our Mutual Friend.
literary_significance: Oliver Twist made the workhouse and the criminal child national subjects and established the 'condition-of-England' subject matter that Dickens, Gaskell, Kingsley and Disraeli developed through the 1840s. Its serialisation in a magazine alongside its author's other novel pioneered the double market of the Victorian writer.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in Bentley's Miscellany from February 1837 to April 1839 and issued in three volumes by Richard Bentley in 1838; the 1846 edition first carried the short title alone with the author's name on it. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Nicholas Nickleby
alternative_titles: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from March 1838 to October 1839, and the novel with which Dickens attacked the Yorkshire 'cheap schools' — the subject of his journey to Yorkshire with Hablot Browne in January-February 1838 in the company of the schoolmaster's son who had exposed them.
plot_or_argument: After the failure of his father's speculation, Nicholas is placed as usher at Dotheboys Hall under Wackford Squeers, rescues the abused boy Smike, and flees with him to London; the two fall in with the theatrical manager Vincent Crummles and his company, and then with the Cheeryble brothers, whose charity sets Nicholas up in business. The subplot of Kate Nickleby's persecution by Sir Mulberry Hawk and of Ralph Nickleby's financial villainy is resolved when Ralph's ruin and suicide follow the revelation of Smike's parentage and the collapse of his schemes.
narrative_structure: Monthly-part narrative moving between three milieux — the school, the theatre and the City — with a subplot of female persecution and a resolved inheritance plot.
principal_characters: Nicholas Nickleby; Smike; Wackford Squeers; Ralph Nickleby; Kate Nickleby; Vincent Crummles; Newman Noggs; the Cheeryble brothers; Sir Mulberry Hawk
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Yorkshire schools, the theatrical touring company of the 1830s, the counting-house and the speculative economy of the late 1830s; the novel appeared during the Chartist agitation and the Anti-Corn Law League's first campaigns.
literary_significance: Nicholas Nickleby ended the cheap boarding-school and did more than any single book to make the treatment of children a public question; the Crummles chapters are the fullest account in Victorian fiction of the provincial theatre, and the novel consolidated Dickens's comic and melodramatic range.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from April 1838 to October 1839, and in three volumes in 1839; the full title is The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Old Curiosity Shop
description: Serialised weekly in Master Humphrey's Clock from April 1840 to February 1841, and the book that produced the 'Bozmania' of 1841: the death of Little Nell was awaited as a public event, and readers in New York reportedly met the arriving ship to ask whether she had died.
plot_or_argument: Nell Trent lives with her grandfather in the Old Curiosity Shop; the old man's gambling debts to the dwarf Quilp drive the pair to flee London, and they wander through the industrial Midlands, a travelling waxwork show, a school and a decayed church, pursued by Quilp and by Nell's brother Fred. They find refuge with the schoolmaster in a village, where Nell dies; the grandfather dies soon after, Quilp is drowned, and Kit Nubbles is rewarded for his fidelity.
narrative_structure: Weekly-part narrative of flight and pursuit, with two parallel plots (Nell's pilgrimage and the Brasses' legal villainy) that meet at the close.
principal_characters: Nell Trent; the grandfather; Daniel Quilp; Kit Nubbles; Dick Swiveller; the Marchioness; Sampson and Sally Brass; Fred Trent; the schoolmaster
literary_form: Novel in weekly parts (Master Humphrey's Clock)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The 1840 gambling houses and the new railway that was beginning to empty the coaching roads; the industrial Midlands seen through the Black Country furnace fires; the periodical market created by Master Humphrey's Clock, in which Dickens tried to revive the eighteenth-century essay-serial.
literary_significance: The Old Curiosity Shop made sentimentality a mass literary emotion and demonstrated the commercial power of the serial death. Its structure — a pilgrimage through English social types in search of a refuge — is the model for the later 'dark' novels' journeys, and the pairing of Nell with Quilp established Dickens's technique of moral contrast through physical grotesque.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published weekly in Master Humphrey's Clock (1840-41) and issued separately in 1841, together with Barnaby Rudge, the two novels that filled that periodical. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Barnaby Rudge: A Tale of the Riots of 'Eighty
description: Dickens's first historical novel, serialised in Master Humphrey's Clock in 1841 and set in 1775-80, with the Gordon Riots of June 1780 as its centrepiece. It is a prose fiction work of 1841 by Charles Dickens; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Serial and Monthly-Part Novel and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The novel braids three plots: the murder of Reuben Haredale and the false accusation of his gardener, the disappearance of Emma Haredale's brother and the villainy of Sir John Chester, and the domestic tragedy of the locksmith Gabriel Varden and his apprentice Sim Tappertit. Barnaby Rudge, an 'innocent' with a pet raven, is swept up in the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots, which the novel narrates as an anatomy of mob violence; the riots end with the storming of Newgate and the burning of the distillery, and the plots are unravelled by Lord George Gordon's trial and Chester's death.
narrative_structure: Double historical plot (private murder and public riot) braided across five years, narrated in weekly installments that culminate in the riot sequence.
principal_characters: Barnaby Rudge; Gabriel Varden; Dolly Varden; Sim Tappertit; Sir John Chester; Edward Chester; Emma Haredale; Geoffrey Haredale; Lord George Gordon; Hugh; Grip the raven
literary_form: Historical novel (Master Humphrey's Clock, weekly parts)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Gordon Riots of 1780, the anti-Catholic agitation that followed the Relief Act of 1778, and the memory of mob violence revived for a Chartist-era readership by the Newport rising of 1839; Dickens drew on the contemporary pamphlet and trial literature for the crowd scenes.
literary_significance: Barnaby Rudge is the first English novel to treat the urban crowd as an organised political phenomenon, and its account of the Gordon Riots is the most sustained piece of crowd-writing in Victorian fiction before A Tale of Two Cities. It is also Dickens's fullest study of the 'idiot' figure whose innocence is at the mercy of public violence.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published weekly in Master Humphrey's Clock (1841) and issued separately the same year; the full title is Barnaby Rudge: A Tale of the Riots of 'Eighty. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Martin Chuzzlewit
alternative_titles: The Life and Adventures of Martin Chuzzlewit
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from January 1843 to July 1844; sales fell so sharply that Dickens's publishers renegotiated his contract, and Dickens responded by sending his hero to America, using the novel to settle scores from his 1842 American tour.
plot_or_argument: Old Martin Chuzzlewit, convinced that his relatives are waiting for his money, has taken in the orphan Mary Graham as a companion; his grandson Martin is disinherited for falling in love with her. Martin is articled to the architect Seth Pecksniff, whose hypocrisy and whose daughters Cherry and Merry drive the plot of self-interest, and he leaves for America with Mark Tapley, where the Eden land-scheme swindle and the comic Americans (Colonel Diver, Mrs Hominy, Hannibal Chollop) expose a fraudulent democracy. The novel's darker plot is the murder of Montague Tigg by Jonas Chuzzlewit, and the resolution restores the repentant Martin to his grandfather's favour.
narrative_structure: Two-part narrative: the English plot of inheritance and hypocrisy, and the American interlude of the Eden settlement, joined by the Tigg murder plot.
principal_characters: Martin Chuzzlewit; old Martin Chuzzlewit; Seth Pecksniff; Mark Tapley; Sairey Gamp; Betsey Prig; Jonas Chuzzlewit; Montague Tigg; Mary Graham; Tom Pinch; Mrs Hominy
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The American tour of 1842 and the copyright agitation, the land speculation of the western boom, the architectural profession and the 'restoration' of churches, and the insolvency and insurance fraud of the early 1840s.
literary_significance: Martin Chuzzlewit contains the most famous English satire of the United States before the twentieth century — the Eden swindle, Mrs Hominy and the 'Chuzzlewit' contempt for American manners — and it produced one of Dickens's great comic inventions in Pecksniff and Sairey Gamp, the nurse whose name became a byword for the drunken professional.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from January 1843 to July 1844, with plates by 'Phiz'; the American chapters were added after the author's 1842 visit and provoked a controversy in the American press. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Dombey and Son
alternative_titles: Dealings with the Firm of Dombey and Son
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from October 1846 to April 1848, the first novel of Dickens's maturity and the first in which the railway enters as a structural and symbolic force. It is a prose fiction work of 1848 by Charles Dickens; it belongs to Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel and it is catalogued here under Serial and Monthly-Part Novel; Industrial and Condition-of-England Novel and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Mr Dombey, of the shipping house Dombey and Son, despises his daughter Florence and invests all his pride in his son Paul, who dies at Dr Blimber's school. Dombey's second marriage, to the proud Edith Granger, collapses when she elopes with his manager Carker, who is killed by a train at the novel's climax; Dombey is ruined by Carker's speculations, and is restored only by Florence's return with her husband Walter Gay and her child.
narrative_structure: Monthly-part narrative organised around the firm of Dombey and Son, with a double movement of loss (Paul, Florence) and recovery, and the railway as the machine of retribution.
principal_characters: Mr Dombey; Florence Dombey; Paul Dombey; Edith Granger; Carker; Walter Gay; Solomon Gills; Captain Cuttle; Susan Nipper; Major Bagstock; Dr Blimber; Polly Toodle
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The railway mania of 1845-47 and the collapse of speculative finance, the shipping house and the counting-house, and the new professional schools and nursing of the 1840s; the novel's railway death is the first great literary use of the train as an instrument of fate.
literary_significance: Dombey and Son marks the turn from the comic picaresque of the early novels to the symbolic structure of the later ones, and its treatment of the father-daughter relation is the first full statement of Dickens's great subject — the damage done by the failure to love. The railway in the novel became a permanent feature of Victorian literary iconography.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from October 1846 to April 1848, with plates by 'Phiz'; the full title is Dealings with the Firm of Dombey and Son, Wholesale, Export, and Oversea. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: David Copperfield
alternative_titles: The Personal History of David Copperfield the Younger
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from May 1849 to November 1850, and the most autobiographical of the novels: the blacking warehouse, the Marshsea debtor's prison, the Murdstone severity of his early schooling and the courtship of Maria Beadnell are all worked into it.
plot_or_argument: David Copperfield is born after his father's death, is sent by his stepfather Murdstone to Salem House and then to the warehouse, runs away to his aunt Betsey Trotwood at Dover, and is educated at Canterbury under Dr Strong while lodging with the Wickfields. He becomes a proctor, falls in love with and marries the childlike Dora Spenlow, loses her, and after the exposure of Uriah Heep's fraud and the shipwreck of Ham and Steerforth, finds his second and mature marriage with Agnes Wickfield. The Micawber and Peggotty strands carry the comic and the emigrant plots (Micawber to Australia, the Peggottys to Australia).
narrative_structure: First-person retrospective narrative in three phases — childhood, youth, maturity — with the Micawber and Peggotty strands acting as comic and moral counterplots.
principal_characters: David Copperfield; Clara Copperfield; Mr Murdstone; Betsey Trotwood; Peggotty; Mr Peggotty; Little Em'ly; Ham; Steerforth; Uriah Heep; Mr Wickfield; Agnes Wickfield; Dora Spenlow; Mr Micawber; Mrs Micawber; Tommy Traddles; Mr Dick
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers); 'the favourite child' of its author
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The 1820s-40s: the debtor's prison and the blacking warehouse, the Doctors' Commons proctorate, the emigrant ships to Australia (the colony as the destination of the failed and the disgraced), and the professionalisation of authorship.
literary_significance: David Copperfield is the founding English Bildungsroman and the model for the autobiographical novel of the later nineteenth and twentieth centuries, from Great Expectations to Sons and Lovers and Joyce's Portrait. Its serial audience was the widest Dickens ever had, and it was the book he chose to read in public to the end of his life.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from May 1849 to November 1850, with plates by 'Phiz'; the full title is The Personal History, Adventures, Experience and Observation of David Copperfield the Younger of Blunderstone Rookery. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Bleak House
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from March 1852 to September 1853, the first of the great 'dark' novels, and the most technically ambitious: two narrators alternate, Esther Summerson in the first person and an unnamed third-person narrator in the present tense, and the Court of Chancery presides over both.
plot_or_argument: Jarndyce and Jarndyce, a Chancery suit over a contested will, has consumed generations of litigants; its costs finally consume the whole estate at the close. Esther Summerson, raised by the harsh Mrs Rachael and sent for by John Jarndyce as companion to his young cousins Richard Carstone and Ada Clare, discovers in the course of the novel that she is the illegitimate daughter of Lady Dedlock, whose secret the lawyer Tulkinghorn discovers and is murdered for; the murder is solved by Inspector Bucket, the first police detective in English fiction. Lady Dedlock dies at the pauper graveyard where her lover is buried, Richard dies of the Chancery suit, and Esther marries Woodcourt.
narrative_structure: Alternating first-person (Esther) and third-person present-tense narration, with the Chancery suit as the master plot and the Dedlock secret as the withheld centre.
principal_characters: Esther Summerson; Lady Dedlock; Sir Leicester Dedlock; John Jarndyce; Harold Skimpole; Richard Carstone; Ada Clare; Inspector Bucket; Tulkinghorn; Mr Guppy; Jo; Krook; Smallweed; Allan Woodcourt; Caddy Jellyby; Mrs Jellyby
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Court of Chancery and the legal profession in the 1840s-50s, the sanitary reform campaign that followed the 1848 cholera epidemic (the death of Jo the crossing-sweeper is the novel's political centre), the metropolitan police detective branch, and the railway and the new suburb.
literary_significance: Bleak House is the most complete Victorian indictment of institutional England and the technical masterpiece of the Victorian multiplot novel; it brought the detective into English fiction and the public-health question into the novel. Its double narration is a permanent model for the novel of contested knowledge, and the opening fog paragraph is among the most analysed passages in English fiction.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from March 1852 to September 1853, with plates by 'Phiz'; the novel alternates a third-person narration with the first-person account of Esther Summerson. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Hard Times. For These Times
description: Serialised in Household Words from 1 April to 12 August 1854 and published in one volume the same year: the shortest of the major novels and the most concentrated attack on utilitarianism in English fiction.
plot_or_argument: In the cotton town of Coketown, Thomas Gradgrind educates his children Louisa and Tom on 'facts'; Louisa marries the manufacturer Josiah Bounderby, the self-made 'Humbug' of the novel, and nearly elopes with the political adventurer James Harthouse before returning to her father's house broken. Tom robs the bank and is exposed by the circus girl Sissy Jupe's circle; Stephen Blackpool, the hand-loom weaver, is falsely accused, refuses to join the union, and dies down a mine shaft; Rachael nurses him, and the circus, with its horse-riding and its 'fancy', stands against the school of fact.
narrative_structure: Three-book structure (Sowing, Reaping, Garnering) with a narrow cast and a plot built on the contrast of two systems of education and two philosophies of life.
principal_characters: Thomas Gradgrind; Louisa Gradgrind; Tom Gradgrind; Josiah Bounderby; Stephen Blackpool; Rachael; James Harthouse; Sissy Jupe; Mrs Sparsit; Bitzer
literary_form: Novel in weekly parts (Household Words); single volume 1854
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Preston strike of 1853-54, which Dickens reported for Household Words, the 1840s-50s factory system and the Ten Hours agitation, and the utilitarian education of the Mechanics' Institutes and the monitorial schools.
literary_significance: Hard Times is the classic Victorian novel of industrial capitalism and the definitive literary critique of utilitarianism; it is the shortest and most taught of Dickens's novels and has been central to the criticism of Victorian ideology from Leavis to the Marxist and postcolonial readings of our own time.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised weekly in Household Words from 1 April to 12 August 1854 and issued in one volume the same year; it is the only one of the author's novels first published in a weekly periodical and without plates. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Little Dorrit
description: Published in nineteen monthly parts from December 1855 to June 1857, the most sombre of the novels and the one that converts the bureaucratic inertia of the 1850s into a whole imaginative system: the Circumlocution Office, the Marshalsea debtor's prison, and the 'Nobody's Fault' of the Merdle speculation.
plot_or_argument: Arthur Clennam returns from twenty years in China to find his mother's house inhabited by the seamstress Amy Dorrit, whose father William Dorrit has been imprisoned in the Marshalsea for twenty-three years. The Dorrits are discovered to be heirs to a fortune and leave the prison only to be destroyed by it mentally; the fortune is lost in the collapse of Merdle's bank, and Clennam is imprisoned in the same Marshalsea for debt. The novel resolves through the collapse of the house of Clennam's secret and the marriage of Arthur and Amy.
narrative_structure: Two interlocked plots — the Dorrit inheritance and the Clennam secret — mediated by the institutional spaces of the Marshalsea and the Circumlocution Office; monthly-part structure with a late revelation.
principal_characters: Amy Dorrit; William Dorrit; Arthur Clennam; Mrs Clennam; Jeremiah Flintwinch; Affery; Mr Merdle; Edmund Sparkler; Henry Gowan; Daniel Doyce; Mr Pancks; Casby; Rigaud; John Chivery; Maggy
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Crimean War and the administrative scandals it exposed, the 'Circumlocution Office' of the permanent civil service, the bankruptcy law and the Marshalsea, and the speculative mania of the 1850s that culminated in the failure of the Royal British Bank in 1856.
literary_significance: Little Dorrit is the great Victorian novel of bureaucracy and of debt, and its Circumlocution Office entered the language as the name of institutional obstruction. Its analysis of the 'Merdle' collapse precedes the financial crises of the later century, and the prison as a metaphor of society is carried further here than anywhere else in Dickens.

bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from December 1855 to June 1857, with plates by 'Phiz'; the novel is divided into the two books 'Poverty' and 'Riches'. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: A Tale of Two Cities
description: Serialised in the first issue of All the Year Round (30 April 1859) and published in one volume in the same year: Dickens's second historical novel, set in London and Paris between 1775 and 1793, and the most widely read of all his books.
plot_or_argument: Dr Manette, released after eighteen years in the Bastille, is reunited with his daughter Lucie in London; Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat who has renounced his title, marries Lucie, and returns to revolutionary Paris to save an old servant, where he is condemned by the revolutionary tribunal through the denunciation of the Defarges. Sydney Carton, who loves Lucie, takes Darnay's place at the guillotine, and the novel closes with his prophecy of a redeemed Paris.
narrative_structure: Historical novel in three books (Recalled to Life, The Golden Thread, The Track of a Storm) with a symmetrical London-Paris plot and a substitution climax.
principal_characters: Sydney Carton; Charles Darnay; Lucie Manette; Dr Alexandre Manette; Madame Defarge; Ernest Defarge; Miss Pross; Mr Lorry; Jerry Cruncher; the Marquis de Saint Evrémonde; John Barsad
literary_form: Historical novel (All the Year Round, weekly; one volume 1859)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The French Revolution of 1789 and the Terror of 1793, the agrarian distress and the English reform agitation of the late 1850s, and the political economy of the two capitals; the novel's account of the crowd and of revolutionary justice drew on Carlyle's French Revolution.
literary_significance: A Tale of Two Cities is the most widely read historical novel in English and the model for the fictional treatment of revolution as both just and terrible; its opening paragraph and its closing sacrifice are among the most quoted in Victorian prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised weekly in All the Year Round from 30 April to 26 November 1859 and issued in three volumes the same year; it was the first novel the author published in his own weekly journal. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Great Expectations
description: Serialised weekly in All the Year Round from December 1860 to August 1861 and published in three volumes in July 1861; the second great first-person novel and the one in which Dickens rewrote the Bildungsroman as a story of moral education by disillusion.
plot_or_argument: Philip Pirrip, 'Pip', is brought up by his sister and her husband Joe Gargery, the village blacksmith; he is summoned to play at the house of Miss Havisham, who has stopped her clocks at the hour of her desertion and raised the beautiful Estella to break men's hearts. Pip becomes convinced that Miss Havisham is his benefactor and that Estella is intended for him; the arrival of the convict Magwitch reveals that his great expectations have come from a transported felon, and the novel turns into a study of Pip's shame, of Magwitch's devotion, and of the loss of the fortune. The original ending leaves Pip and Estella parted; the published ending gives them a tentative reunion.
narrative_structure: First-person retrospective narrative in three stages of expectation, revelation and correction, with the convict plot displacing the fairy-tale plot at the centre.
principal_characters: Philip Pirrip (Pip); Joe Gargery; Mrs Joe; Magwitch (Provis); Miss Havisham; Estella; Herbert Pocket; Mr Jaggers; Wemmick; Mr Pumblechook; Biddy; Orlick; Compeyson; Clara Barley
literary_form: Novel in weekly parts (All the Year Round); three volumes 1861
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The 1810s-20s of the novel's setting and the 1860s of its composition: the convict hulks and transportation to Australia, the gentleman's education and the idle 'expectations' of the gentry, the counting-house and the trading house, and the working of the criminal law.
literary_significance: Great Expectations is the most perfectly constructed of Dickens's novels and the central English novel about class and shame; its treatment of Pip's gentlemanly self-invention and of Magwitch's colonial fortune made it a foundational text for later postcolonial and class criticism, and its two endings are a permanent case study in narrative authority.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised weekly in All the Year Round from 1 December 1860 to 3 August 1861 and issued in three volumes in 1861; the serial form obliged the author to shorten his first design. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Our Mutual Friend
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from May 1864 to November 1865, the last completed novel and the darkest of the London books: its dust-heaps, its river and its schoolmaster's 'whosoever' frame a satire on inheritance, money and the new finance.
plot_or_argument: Old Harmon, a dust-contractor, leaves his fortune to his son John on condition that he marry Bella Wilfer, a girl he has never met; the son is reported drowned, and the will's legacy passes to the Boffins, the old servant and his wife. John Harmon returns under the name John Rokesmith as Boffin's secretary, tests Bella's character by pretending to miserliness, and reveals himself at the close. The other plots are the murder of the waterman Hexam by Bradley Headstone, the love of Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie Hexam, and the satirical career of the Veneerings and the Podsnaps.
narrative_structure: Multiplot monthly-part narrative organised by the river and the dust-heap as its two governing images, with the Harmon inheritance as the master plot.
principal_characters: John Harmon (John Rokesmith); Bella Wilfer; Nicodemus Boffin; Mrs Boffin; Silas Wegg; Mr Venus; Lizzie Hexam; Charley Hexam; Gaffer Hexam; Eugene Wrayburn; Bradley Headstone; Mortimer Lightwood; Mr Podsnap; the Veneerings; Jenny Wren; Riah; Fledgeby
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The Thames as the city's sewer and its source of wealth, the dust-contractors and the new money of the 1860s, the spread of the joint-stock company and the limited liability of the Companies Act (1862), and the school system of the pupil-teacher and the training college.
literary_significance: Our Mutual Friend is Dickens's last complete statement on money, class and the river, and it contains his most sustained satire of the nouveaux riches and of the education system; its imagery of dust and water has been central to the modern critical reading of Dickens, and it is the novel in which his late style reaches its most elliptical.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in twenty monthly numbers from May 1864 to November 1865, with plates by Marcus Stone; it was the last of the novels completed by its author. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Mystery of Edwin Drood
description: Dickens's last novel, of which only six of the twelve projected monthly numbers were published (April-September 1870) before his death on 9 June; the remaining part of the sixth number was in proof. It is the most famous unfinished novel in English, and the central problem of its criticism is the disappearance of Edwin Drood.
plot_or_argument: John Jasper, the choirmaster of Cloisterham, is an opium addict in love with his nephew Edwin Drood's betrothed, Rosa Bud. Edwin disappears on Christmas Eve after a quarrel with Neville Landless; a watch and a scarf-pin are found in the river, and Jasper accuses Neville. The novel's remaining numbers introduce the twin themes of the opium den and the Cathedral close, and Dickens's own notes and the surviving plans have been used ever since to argue whether Jasper murdered Edwin.
narrative_structure: Twelve projected monthly numbers of which six survive; the extant text ends mid-number with the discovery of the watch and pin.
principal_characters: John Jasper; Edwin Drood; Rosa Bud; Neville Landless; Helena Landless; Mr Grewgious; Mr Crisparkle; Durdles; Deputy; the Princess Puffer; Mr Honeythunder; Mr Bazzard
literary_form: Unfinished novel in monthly parts (6 of 12 numbers published)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The cathedral close of Rochester (Cloisterham), the opium trade and the East India Company's traffic, and the Anglo-Indian characters (Neville and Helena Landless) that Dickens drew from his 1869-70 reading tour and his interest in the colonies.
literary_significance: The Mystery of Edwin Drood inaugurated the Detective Club tradition of the 'unfinished mystery', and it has generated a whole literature of solutions (from Cuming Walters to the modern attribution scholarship). It is also the clearest evidence of the direction Dickens's late art was taking — towards the short, tightly plotted, symbolically dense novel of crime.
attribution_notes: Unfinished at the author's death; the surviving text is the first six numbers only. All completions and solutions after 1870 are by other hands.
bibliographical_notes: Issued by Chapman and Hall in monthly numbers from April 1870; six of the twelve projected numbers appeared before the author's death on 9 June 1870, and the novel remains a fragment. The research status is partial. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas
alternative_titles: Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas
description: Published on 19 December 1843, the first of the five Christmas books, and the one that fixed the Victorian Christmas and the modern image of Scrooge; it sold 6,000 copies in a week and has never been out of print.
plot_or_argument: Ebenezer Scrooge, the miser of a counting-house, is visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his partner Jacob Marley and then by the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come, who show him his own childhood, the Cratchit family and the death of Tiny Tim, and his own unmourned death. He wakes on Christmas morning transformed, sends a turkey to the Cratchits, and becomes 'as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew'.
narrative_structure: Five-stave structure (staves, in place of chapters), a dream-vision frame with three visitations and a conversion ending.
principal_characters: Ebenezer Scrooge; Bob Cratchit; Tiny Tim; Jacob Marley; Fred; Belle; Fan; Fezziwig; the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is innumerable proper names that carry character as epithet (Pecksniff, Gradgrind, Bounderby, Scrooge, Uriah Heep, Mr F's Aunt).
historical_context: The 1843 report of the Children's Employment Commission on the mines and manufactures, which Dickens had read in October 1843 and intended to answer with a pamphlet before he chose fiction instead; the new Christmas annual market and the Victorian reinvention of the festival.
literary_significance: A Christmas Carol created the modern Christmas story and the secular morality of Christmas giving, and it was Dickens's most effective single act of social persuasion. It is also the founding text of the English ghost story as a vehicle of moral argument.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Boz. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London by Chapman and Hall on 19 December 1843, in an edition with hand-coloured etchings by John Leech; the first edition sold out before Christmas and the book has never been out of print. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Vanity Fair: A Novel without a Hero
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from January 1847 to July 1848, with Thackeray's own illustrations, and subtitled 'A Novel without a Hero': the great English novel of the 1810s-20s seen from the vantage of the 1840s, and the book that fixed the word 'snob' and the phrase 'vanity fair' in the language.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows two schoolfellows from Miss Pinkerton's academy: Amelia Sedley, the sentimental and self-deceiving daughter of a rich City merchant, and Becky Sharp, the penniless governess who determines to make her fortune. Amelia marries George Osborne, who is killed at Waterloo, and later the faithful, self-sacrificing William Dobbin; Becky marries Rawdon Crawley, becomes the favourite of the jealous Miss Crawley, is received into the highest society and then ruined by her intrigue with Lord Steyne, and ends as a respectable pensioner of Jos Sedley. The Waterloo section, the Brussels chapters, and the final fair scenes are the novel's set pieces.
narrative_structure: Panoramic third-person narrative in twenty monthly parts, with a narrator who comments from the vantage of 1848 on the events of 1813-30, and a 'before and after the curtain' frame.
principal_characters: Becky Sharp; Amelia Sedley; George Osborne; William Dobbin; Rawdon Crawley; Miss Crawley; Lord Steyne; Jos Sedley; Mr Sedley; Sir Pitt Crawley; Miss Briggs
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers, 1847-48); one volume 1848
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The Regency and the Napoleonic wars, the Battle of Waterloo, the City bankruptcy of 1815-16, the marriage market of the gentry, and the India service and the colonial fortune; the novel is also a satire on the 1840s readership that consumed it.
literary_significance: Vanity Fair is the central English novel of social satire in the nineteenth century and the definitive portrait of the adventuress. Becky Sharp is the first great female anti-heroine in English fiction, and the novel's refusal of a moralising ending made it a permanent point of reference for the ironic novel from Meredith to Thackeray's modernist readers.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1848, by William Makepeace Thackeray. Composed between 1847 and 1848. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The History of Pendennis: His Fortunes and Misfortunes, His Friends and His Greatest Enemy
alternative_titles: History of Pendennis: His Fortunes and Misfortunes, His Friends and His Greatest Enemy
description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from November 1848 to December 1850, a semi-autobiographical Bildungsroman of a young gentleman of the 1830s-40s and the first of Thackeray's novels to be set in his own century.
plot_or_argument: Arthur Pendennis, the son of a West Country doctor's widow, goes up to Oxbridge, gets into debt, is jilted in his first love for the actress Emily Fotheringay, and comes to London to read for the bar and to write for the press. His uncle Major Pendennis manages his social career and the family's fortune, and after a period of dissipation and a broken engagement to Blanche Amory, he marries his childhood friend Laura Bell and settles into the life of a country gentleman and a successful novelist.
narrative_structure: The work is in 24 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Arthur Pendennis; Helen Pendennis; Major Pendennis; Laura Bell; Emily Fotheringay; Blanche Amory; George Warrington; Harry Foker; Dr Portman; Costigan
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s: the Regency survivors who manage the young man's career, the press as a profession for gentlemen, the debts and bailiffs of the 'swell', and the literary market that Thackeray himself inhabited.
literary_significance: Pendennis is the most directly autobiographical of Thackeray's novels and the fullest English account of the making of a gentleman and a professional writer in the 1840s; it established the 'novel of a young man's education' as a vehicle for social criticism that Dickens, Trollope and Meredith all used.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1850, as novel in monthly parts (24 numbers), by William Makepeace Thackeray. Composed between 1848 and 1850. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The History of Henry Esmond, Esq., a Colonel in the Service of Her Majesty Queen Anne. Written by Himself
alternative_titles: History of Henry Esmond, Esq., a Colonel in the Service of Her Majesty Queen Anne. Written by Himself
description: Published in three volumes in 1852 and set in the reign of Queen Anne (1702-14): Thackeray's masterly historical novel, written throughout in the idiom of the early eighteenth century, and the only one of his books to sustain a single voice from beginning to end.
plot_or_argument: Henry Esmond, a foundling of the Castlewood family who believes himself to be illegitimate, serves as a soldier under Marlborough in Flanders and as a man of letters in London, falling in love with his cousin Beatrix, who prefers the young Pretender. He marries Rachel, Lady Castlewood, who is in fact the mother of the true heir and whom he has loved since boyhood, and they emigrate to Virginia, where the novel's frame places the aged Esmond and his descendants.
narrative_structure: A novel issued in monthly parts, each part carrying its own set piece and closing on a suspension, the parts gathered afterwards into the volume. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Henry Esmond; Rachel, Lady Castlewood; Beatrix Esmond; Francis Esmond; the second Viscount Castlewood; Lord Mohun; the Duke of Hamilton; Swift; Steele; Addison; Colonel Esmond
literary_form: Historical novel in the first person
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The War of the Spanish Succession and the campaigns of Queen Anne, the Jacobite succession crisis, the death of Anne and the Hanoverian accession of 1714, and the London of Addison, Steele and Swift. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1852 and first published in 1852 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under serial and monthly-part novel; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Henry Esmond is the finest historical novel of the eighteenth century written in the nineteenth, and its archaised first-person narration — Thackeray's most sustained experiment in style — has been a permanent model for the historical novel in the first person, from Scott's and Thackeray's heirs to the historical fiction of the twentieth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1852, as historical novel in the first person, by William Makepeace Thackeray. Composed between 1851 and 1852. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family
alternative_titles: Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family
description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from October 1853 to August 1855, narrated by Arthur Pendennis, and the most encompassing of Thackeray's family chronicles: the history of the Newcome family from the Indian fortune of the 'Campaigner' to the ruin of the banker Barnes Newcome.
plot_or_argument: Clive Newcome, an artist, loves his cousin Ethel Newcome, who is pressed by her family into the marriage market; the novel follows the family's fortunes through the colonial service, the City bank, the influence of the evangelical 'Bungay' faction and the collapse of the bank of Hobson Brothers. Clive marries Rosey Mackenzie and is widowed, and Ethel remains unmarried in a resolution that the narrator leaves deliberately unresolved.
narrative_structure: The work is in 24 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Clive Newcome; Ethel Newcome; Colonel Thomas Newcome; Barnes Newcome; Sir Brian Newcome; Lady Ann Newcome; Rosey Mackenzie; Arthur Pendennis; the Campaigner; Fred Bayham
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The 1830s-50s: the City bank and its failure, the Anglo-Indian family, the marriage market of the upper middle class, and the evangelical philanthropy of the second generation. The record dates the work as composed between 1853 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Victorian Realism and the Novel of Ordinary Life, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; serial and monthly-part novel.
literary_significance: The Newcomes is Thackeray's most sympathetic book and the most complete picture of the Victorian family across three generations; its portrait of Ethel Newcome as a woman with no independent income and no independent will is one of the period's sharpest studies of the position of women, and its phrase 'the most respectable family' became a byword for respectable hypocrisy.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1855, as novel in monthly parts (24 numbers), by William Makepeace Thackeray. Composed between 1853 and 1855. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Virginians: A Tale of the Last Century
alternative_titles: Virginians: A Tale of the Last Century
description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from November 1857 to October 1859, the sequel to Henry Esmond and the first English novel to treat the American Revolution from the perspective of a Virginian family divided by it.
plot_or_argument: Henry and George Warrington, grandsons of Henry Esmond, grow up in Virginia; the novel follows Harry's extravagant progress through London society while George is believed killed in Braddock's defeat, George's return from a French prison, the brothers' marriages, and the War of Independence, which divides the brothers between the colonial cause and the Crown. The novel's history is deliberately digressive and its plot subordinate to the panorama of the 1750s-70s.
narrative_structure: The work is in 24 numbers. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel issued in monthly parts, each part carrying its own set piece and closing on a suspension, the parts gathered afterwards into the volume.
principal_characters: George Warrington; Harry Warrington; Rachel Esmond Warrington (Madam Esmond), their mother; Baroness Bernstein (the former Beatrix Esmond); Lady Maria Esmond; General Lambert; Theo Lambert; Hetty Lambert; Fanny Mountain; George Washington
literary_form: Historical novel in monthly parts (24 numbers)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The Seven Years' War, the American Revolution, the London of the 1750s and the literary world of Fielding and Johnson, and the Virginia plantation economy of the eighteenth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1857 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under serial and monthly-part novel; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: The Virginians is the most substantial English novel of the American Revolution and the fullest picture in Victorian fiction of the transatlantic family; its treatment of the colonial gentleman's divided loyalty is a significant document in the nineteenth-century English imagination of America.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1859, as historical novel in monthly parts (24 numbers), by William Makepeace Thackeray. Composed between 1857 and 1859. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Book of Snobs
description: A series of sketches published in Punch in 1846-47 and collected in 1848: a taxonomy of English snobbery — the country snob, the city snob, the military snob, the clerical snob, the literary snob — written in the person of a satirical observer who includes himself among the objects of the analysis.
plot_or_argument: The book has no narrative. It proceeds by category and example, with mock-learned definitions and illustrative anecdotes, and it closes with an account of 'the snob royal' and the observation that 'the world is a snobbish world'.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The 1840s, the decade of the railway and the new money, the club and the dinner party, and the Punch humour of Douglas Jerrold, Lemon and Thackeray himself. title: The Four Georges
description: Four lectures on the Hanoverian kings, delivered in the United States in 1855-56 and in Britain from 1856, and published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1860 and as a book in 1861: a satire on the House of Hanover that works by the accumulation of trivial detail and by the contrast between the king's private life and the public pageant.

description: Six lectures on Swift, Congreve, Addison and Steele, Pope, Hogarth, Smollett, Fielding, Sterne and Goldsmith, delivered in 1851 and published in 1853: the Victorian century's most influential account of the English eighteenth century, and a manifesto for the comic-satirical tradition that Thackeray claimed as his own.
